query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloys, elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and stability of protective oxide scales that are sensitive to the oxygen partial pressure. Specifically, in oxidizing environments, a coherent, adherent oxide scale rich in Al and Cr forms and protects the fcc substrate, whereas in reducing atmospheres, the limited or disrupted oxide formation leads to scale spallation and accelerated substrate degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy retaining an fcc matrix with fixed processing history.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled high-temperature (approximately 800 °C) cyclic oxidation tests in gas atmospheres with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures, including pure oxygen, standard air, and reducing conditions (by adding H2 or CO to air).
generation.conditions: Testing at around 800 °C under cyclic oxidation exposure over durations sufficient to observe scale formation (up to ~100 hours) while holding the alloy composition and processing constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, thickness, and adhesion of the oxide scale—primarily formed of Al- and Cr-rich compounds—mediate the degradation process by either protecting the substrate or failing under reducing conditions.
generation.mechanism: The oxygen availability in the gas atmosphere drives the formation of a protective oxide scale. In oxidizing environments, sufficient oxygen leads to the formation of a stable, adherent Al/Cr oxide scale that mitigates degradation. In reducing conditions, inadequate oxygen supply prevents the development of a protective scale or leads to its breakdown, resulting in enhanced scale spallation and accelerated substrate oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed under high oxygen partial pressures will develop a uniform, well-adhered oxide layer with slower degradation rates, whereas samples in reducing atmospheres will show thinner, discontinuous oxide scales with greater tendencies for spallation and higher degradation rates compared to the baseline behavior in standard air.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior as observed under standard ambient air at 800 °C, where a balance between scale formation and limited spallation is initially achieved.
generation.boundary: Observations are limited to an exposure temperature of around 800 °C and exposure durations that do not introduce phase transformations beyond the stable fcc matrix, ensuring that the measured effects are due purely to variations in the gas atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: While the directional influence of oxygen partial pressure on the formation and stability of protective oxide scales is expected, the precise quantitative differences in degradation rates and scale characteristics require experimental validation due to potential synergistic elemental effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples. Divide them into three groups and expose each group at 800 °C under cyclic oxidation conditions in: (a) pure oxygen atmosphere, (b) standard air, and (c) a reducing atmosphere (air with controlled H2 or CO additions). After predetermined intervals (e.g., every 20 hours up to 100 hours), perform detailed surface and cross-sectional analyses.
measurements: Scale composition and phase analysis (using XRD and EDS)
Extent of scale adhesion versus spallation (quantified by spallation tests or image analysis)
Microstructural changes beneath the oxide scale (using TEM if necessary)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments reveal no systematic variation in the scale morphology, thickness, or adhesion—and consequently similar degradation rates—across the different oxygen partial pressures, then the hypothesis that oxygen partial pressure governs the degradation mechanism via protective oxide scale formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.

The latter synergy also improved the oxidation kinetics in JZ3+ compared with the Ta and W free alloy OHS1 (parabolic + linear in OHS1, with the kp for the first 3h of oxidation [] similar to that of JZ3+ for the whole duration of the oxidation experiment). In Ti-rich (Ti ≥ 24 at.%) Sn-containing Nb-silicide-based alloys, after isothermal oxidation at 1200 °C there was enrichment in Sn in the substrate at the oxide scale/substrate interface where the compounds Nb3Sn and Nb5Sn2Si were formed [,,,]. The latter intermetallic has W5Si3 as its prototype (the same as βNb5Si3), and is not believed to be stable in the Nb-Si-Sn ternary system at 1200 °C []. The research in [,,,] would suggest that the synergy of Mo and Hf with Al and Cr, and contamination of the alloy by oxygen stabilised the Nb5Sn2Si compound at high temperatures. The Nb5Sn2Si or other TM5Sn2X compounds [] (TM = Nb, Ti, X = Al, Si) were not observed in the alloys JZ2, JZ3 and JZ3+ at 1200 °C (Table 7), which would suggest that the synergy of Sn with Ge, Ta and W did not stabilise these compounds. Segregation of solutes at the substrate just below the scale/substrate interface has been studied in [,,,,] and reported in [].

cited_evidence.text: Zone A formation was observed in the alloy MG7 and layered microstructures formed in the alloys MG7 and OHC5 [,]. Common in all these alloys was the simultaneous presence of Al, Si, and Ti and solute macrosegregation. Note that in the alloy OHC3, which did not contain Si and Ti, a Zone A did not form even though the alloy was Al-rich. Considering the maps in the Figure 8, if Zone A formation in the BC alloy were to be required, the alloy should have δ > 6, VEC > 3.75 and Δχ > 0.1. BC alloys with Al, Cr, Hf, Nb, Si, and Ti-alloying elements compatible with metallic UHTM substrates with Nb and Si addition could be designed/selected to have the parameters δ, VEC, and Δχ in the as-manufactured condition and after exposure to high temperature, respectively, in the ranges 6 < δ < 10.5, 3.75 < VEC < 4.5 and 0.1 < Δχ < 0.16.

Earlier works reported that Fe in RM(Nb)ICs had an effect on the formation of Ti-rich Nbss only when it was in synergy with Cr and 5 at.% Sn (alloy NV5). Nbss was not stable when Al and 5 at.% Sn were in synergy (alloy ZX6), when Hf and 5 at.% Sn were simultaneously present with Al (alloys EZ5 and EZ8) and when Fe was in synergy with 5 at.% Sn with/without Cr (alloys NV5 and NV8). In other words, 5 at.% Sn and specific solutes from the group of the elements Al, Cr, Fe and Hf can support or suppress (1) the formation of Ti-rich Nbss in cast RM(Nb)ICs and (2) the stability of Nbss in the alloys. The data for alloy NV2 would suggest that, with 5 at.% Sn, the concentrations of Al, Fe, Hf, Si and Ti in RM(Nb)ICs could be key for the formation of Ti-rich Nbss and the stability of Nbss.

occupying_moves.conditions: Temperature range of 700–900 °C applied to specimens with fixed composition and processing; comparing exposures in standard air versus atmospheres with controlled variations in oxidizer/reducer ratios to isolate effects previously conflated with phase adjustments

occupying_moves.technique: systematic cyclic oxidation tests coupled with microstructural and compositional analysis (using XRD, SEM-EDS, and possibly TEM)
occupying_moves.conditions: Exposures at ~800 °C in atmospheres ranging from highly oxidizing (pure O2 or O2-rich air) to reducing (with defined H2 or CO additions) while keeping the additive manufacturing processing history constant

chosen.technique: high-temperature cyclic oxidation testing with SEM, EDS, and XRD analysis
chosen.conditions: Specimens are exposed at ~800 °C under systematically varied gas atmospheres (from pure O2 or air to controlled reducing environments using H2 or CO additions) while holding alloy composition and processing constant
chosen.why: This approach directly targets the open question regarding synergistic elemental effects in complex alloys by isolating the role of oxygen availability on the formation and stability of protective oxide scales. It distinguishes the mechanistic hypothesis from previous work that conflated compositional limits, phase transformation, and processing by controlling for these variables and focusing on the gas environment as the key lever. Observations such as a transition from protective scale formation in oxidizing conditions to deleterious scale breakdown in reducing conditions—and deviations from those expected trends—would provide a clear test of the proposed hypothesis, with a lack of such differences falsifying it.
